https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-several-ki.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J7IY Russian missiles hit residential buildings and a medical facility in Kyiv, according to the city administration Image: Anatolii Stepanov/REUTERS Advertisement Overnight Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv , and its surrounding regions killed at least 16 people and injured more than 40, Ukrainian authorities said Thursday. Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said that Moscow had launched a massive ballistic missile attack on the city and that cleanup operations were still underway. He called for Friday to be observed as a day of mourning. What do we know about the Russian attacks? The attacks damaged residential buildings, a medical facility and an educational institution, the Kyiv city military administration said in a statement. The power supply in some parts of the capital was also cut. At least 16 people were killed in Kyiv, officials said. Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent months Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS Klitschko said seven people died in the city's Solomianskyi district, where a fire broke out and the upper floors of a nine-story residential block were destroyed. Which other areas were hit? Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia also attacked gas infrastructure in the northern Chernihiv region and a border crossing with Moldova in the southern Odesa region. "It was ‌a massive ‌attack — the ​Russians had been preparing for a long ​time, combining different types of ⁠ballistic missiles, ​cruise ​missiles, and drones, ​aiming to ‌cause as much damage ​as ⁠possible to civilian infrastructure," ⁠Zelenskyy ​said on social media. Ukraine has a critical shortage of interceptors to down ballistic missiles , a weakness Russia has sought to exploit. The Russian Defense Ministry said it had targeted facilities producing drone components, a military depot and a logistics hub in the attacks on Kyiv and its surrounds. Ukraine faces Patriot missile shortage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In neighboring Poland, the Polish army said it started preventive military aviation operations to protect its airspace amid the Russian strikes. The Polish military often takes this measure amid heavy Russian strikes on Ukraine. In Romania, the Defense Ministry said a drone crashed into an uninhabited area of the country of Tulcea during the Russian attacks. The ministry added that radar systems detected aerial targets near the Ukrainian border, prompting the scrambling of two Spanish fighter jets deployed on NATO missions and a Romanian air force helicopter. A drone also crossed Moldova's airspace, the country's military said. Escalation on both sides Russia has stepped up attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent months, with Ukraine also increasing attacks deep within Russia. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 250 drones had flown toward the Moscow region between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. Diplomatic efforts have failed to reach a ceasefire in the war, which started with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Could deadly strikes inside Russia backfire on Ukraine? https://www.breitbart.com/politics/2026/.text: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov Monday at the G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. A Treasury spokesman told Breitbart News the meeting was about President Trump’s peace deal between Russia and Ukraine. The meeting comes just a week after CIA Director John Ratcliffe met with Russian intelligence officials in Moscow. Both the Kremlin and U.S. officials said little about the discussions. It was the first publicly-known visit to Moscow by the head of the CIA since 2021. An Axios report said that Ratcliffe floated a trilateral meeting between President Trump, Russian President Putin, and Ukrainian President Zelensky in an effort to end the war. Russian attacks on Ukraine have increased in recent days, killing 37 on Saturday, one of the deadliest days of the four-year war. “Right now, Russia’s tactic is to wear down Ukraine and Ukrainians – first and foremost, our people,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on social media late Sunday. The Treasury spokesperson said Monday’s meeting was aimed at discussing President Trump’s plan for peace and economic growth. Bessent has emphasized economic growth as the primary focus of the G20 Finance Minsters meeting, eschewing the Biden-era focus on climate change and net-zero carbon policies. Additionally, Bessent has led Operation Economic Outcast to isolate Iran. The Iranian regime has reportedly received intelligence from Russian officials, and some outlets have reported Russian drone incursions into Romania, a missile that crossed into Poland last month, and an uptick in alleged sabotage actions and cyberattacks in Europe. Breitbart News reported Sunday that the Patriarch of the Greek Orthodox Church, Theophilos III, is planning to embark on a mission to meet both Putin and Zelensky to help find a way to broker an end to the war in Ukraine. http://www.heraldglobe.com/news/27930128.text: Key Russian ally mulls military mobilization RT.com 11 Sep 2026, 22:25 GMT+10 Minsk seeks to shake up its military and get it ready for a potential war, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has said Belarus will bolster its military combat readiness and could even announce "mobilization" to test it, President Alexander Lukashenko has said. The Belarusian leader made the remarks on Friday when he toured the Obuz-Lesnovsky military training grounds near the city of Baranovichi in the west of the country. During his visit, Lukashenko met top military officials and inspected communications and control systems. The president said that he was set to continue vetting the country's forces, revealing that an artillery brigade and signal troops are currently undergoing extensive inspections. "I've already put it in plain terms: the army needs a shake-up - the time has come. The entire army. We will vet everyone. Right up to the point of mobilization," Lukashenko told reporters. The vetting process is set to be as close to real war conditions as possible, he added. "We are preparing for war so that it does not happen," the Belarusian leader stated. Speaking to senior military officials, the president reiterated that Minsk was not seeking to attack anyone but only to bolster its defenses. "We have no intention of attacking anyone; we are pragmatists. We understand that attacking anyone - say, one of our neighbors - would be tantamount to suicide. We cannot win a conflict against the 'monsters' - the states situated along our borders," he said. While it was not immediately clear which countries exactly Lukashenko described as "monsters," most of the Belarusian neighbors' militaries greatly surpass its capabilities. Minsk maintains a modestly sized military of less than 50,000 active-duty servicemen, against some 1.5 million troops in Belarus' key ally, Russia. Ukraine, which has been locked in a conflict with Russia for over four years, is believed to have around 900,000 active-duty personnel. Other neighbors of Belarus, Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia are NATO member states. While the two Baltic nations have tiny militaries, Warsaw has been actively building up its force recently. Poland has some 220,000 active-duty troops and continues to expand the force as well as rearm it with modern weaponry. Numbers-wise, the country's military has become the third-largest within the NATO bloc, surpassed only by the US and Türkiye. https://www.politico.eu/article/serbia-a.text: BELGRADE — Aleksandar Vučić announced the end of his 12-year reign as the most powerful man in Serbia on Sunday following a pivotal election that swept the Student List protest movement to victory. “I want to inform you that, based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections,” Vučić said in an address to journalists and party members at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party in the capital. Vučić said the Student List had secured a majority of between 135 and 140 mandates in the country’s 250-seat parliament, while his own party won 105. Advertisement Advertisement As the minutes ticked by after the polls closed at 8 p.m. local time, the Central Election Commission and election observers remained silent instead of publishing their customary exit results. An hour later, Vučić’s abrupt statement was carried simultaneously on all TV channels in Serbia. The moment the news landed, euphoric residents started streaming into central Belgrade, dancing, hugging and chanting Gotov je! (“He’s finished!”), a refrain popularized a quarter century ago, the last time the country saw this level of voter participation. That October 2000 ballot toppled Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosević following a punishing decade of wars in the Balkans. “Never again to tyranny in our country!” said the leader of the Student List candidates roster, Ilija Srdanović. “We are moving toward a civilized and better Serbia,” he told journalists in an address at the party’s headquarters. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also released a statement after Vučić’s concession, noting that “today, the people of Serbia turned out in record numbers to shape their country’s future” and congratulating the Student List on its victory. “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” she added. While Serbia has been an official EU candidate country since 2012, its candidacy remains frozen over rule-of-law and democracy concerns and Belgrade’s refusal to join EU sanctions on Russia. Advertisement Advertisement Tense hours precede euphoria Turnout hit a near-record 67.8% by 7 p.m., according to independent election monitors CRTA, up from 58.8% in the 2023 general elections. Voters queued for hours on Sunday, including diaspora voters in cities across the world with large Serb populations such as Chicago, Toronto, Vienna and Zurich. Tensions were particularly high in Belgrade after the main street leading to the Central Election Commission was closed off by metal police barriers before noon and armored riot control vehicles rolled into the center. “For the first time in Serbia, access to the CEC by voters was blocked. Average citizens were denied the right to report any kind of irregularity, or even approach the building,” Raša Nedeljkov, program director at CRTA, said after polling stations closed. After the vote ended, the main thoroughfares in front of City Hall and the parliament were also barricaded, and groups of hooded men in dark clothing appeared in front of key institutions along with black police vans. The Student List called on voters not to gather in the center and to avoid physical confrontation. Election observers from the OSCE, the Council of Europe and the European Parliament were on the ground to provide an independent assessment of the electoral process, with the latter being escorted by police. Advertisement Advertisement “We’re sad that it’s come to a point where European Parliament representatives need police protection while going around Belgrade and Serbia,” Nedeljkov added. “Imagine what it’s like for voters.” Vučić served as prime minister from 2014 to 2017 and then held the presidency until resigning in September to lead the progressives into the election. Under his rule Serbia was classed as an electoral autocracy by the Sweden-based V-Dem research institute and only “partly free” by the Washington-based Freedom House advocacy NGO. Reporters Without Borders, which named Vučić a “press freedom predator” in 2025, now ranks Serbia 104th in the world for press freedom, last among the 40 countries in the EU and the Balkans. Sunday’s elections capped two years of protest in Serbia, in which the largest movement in the country’s modern history drew unprecedented support nationwide. The trigger for the unrest was the collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian metropolis of Novi Sad in November 2024 that killed 16 people. A group of university students announced in May last year that they would run in Sunday’s elections and put forward a list of experts to lead the ballot, largely doctors, engineers and other professionals. Vučić’s right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party has repeatedly been criticized by independent watchdogs for overseeing a significant democratic decline in Serbia, including limiting press freedoms and the operation of an independent judiciary.
